title: Yieldedness
hookLine: Anabaptists speak of letting go of self-will

cards: A man is running across a frozen pond in the Netherlands, and behind him runs the man sent to catch him. He is an Anabaptist, and his faith is the charge. He makes it across.
Behind him the ice cracks, and his pursuer goes through into the freezing water. The man stops, turns around, goes back out onto the ice, and pulls the officer out. Then he is taken.
His name was Dirk Willems, and his story is told in the Martyrs Mirror, a book of Anabaptist martyr stories. A new week opens with the Anabaptists and the Quakers, and a German word: Gelassenheit.

teach.b: Gelassenheit is hard to fit into one English word. Yieldedness comes close. Letting go.
Letting be. Among the Amish, the Mennonites, the Hutterites and other Anabaptist churches, it names a whole way of standing in the world: giving up self-will, to God and to the community.
Its pattern is Jesus in the garden the night before he died.
He asks for the cup to pass from him, and then says, "nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Honest about what you want, and still letting go of it.
It shows up in ordinary things: yielding to the church's shared way of life instead of standing out from it.
In some communities plain clothes are part of that, not a costume but a quiet refusal to make the self the point. And it shows up in conflict.
Anabaptist churches teach nonresistance, taking Jesus at his word in the Sermon on the Mount: "resist not evil."

teach.h: HE TURNED BACK ON THE ICE.
teach.b: They hear a call to absorb harm instead of handing it back. Other churches read that verse differently, and teach that defending a neighbor can sometimes be right; Christians have held both views in good faith.
Now go back to the pond. Self-will said keep running. Gelassenheit said turn around.
It sounds like weakness, like giving up. On the ice it looked like the hardest kind of strength.

how: Amish, Mennonite, Hutterite and other Anabaptist Christians speak of Gelassenheit, yielding self-will to God and to the community; it shapes their life together and their teaching of nonresistance.

o: calm detachment, caring about nothing at all
yieldedness: letting go of self-will to God and others
a German word for plain dress and simple living

s: Gelassenheit means not caring about anything
it means letting go of self-will, to God and the community. on the ice it took strength.
Dirk Willems got away and was never caught
he turned back to pull his pursuer out of the ice, and then he was taken.
the story of Dirk Willems is told in the Martyrs Mirror
a book of Anabaptist martyr stories.

games.q: you're Dirk Willems. you've made it across the ice. behind you, the man chasing you falls through. what do you do?
o: keep running; this is your chance.
turn back and pull him out.
shout for help and keep going.
games.why: he goes back and pulls his pursuer out, and then he is taken. the Martyrs Mirror tells it as a life that had already let go.

practice: Bring to mind one disagreement you're in right now, the dishes, a plan, an old argument that keeps coming back, and notice where you want your way.

Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and ask what it would cost to let just this one go. If you pray, you can say Jesus's words from the garden, not my will, but thine; if you don't, simply let your hands stay open.

wordCard.voice: Gelassenheit. The German word Anabaptists use for yieldedness: letting go of self-will, to God and to one another.

carryVoice: Your line: let go. Not losing every argument, just loosening your grip, so your hands are free. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done
